title: Ethernet, MAC, ARP and VLANs: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on how Layer 2 works: Ethernet frames, MAC addresses, switch MAC tables, ARP resolution and caching, VLANs with trunking, and broadcast domains.

chapters.title: Layer 2 Mental Model: Frames, MACs and Switches
points: Ethernet frame layout: Dst MAC (6B) | Src MAC (6B) | EtherType (2B) | Payload (46-1500B) | FCS (4B); the standard MTU of 1500 bytes is the payload limit
EtherType identifies the payload: 0x0800 = IPv4, 0x0806 = ARP, 0x86DD = IPv6, 0x8100 = 802.1Q VLAN tag
MAC address = 48 bits in hex (AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF); first 24 bits are the OUI (vendor), last 24 bits are device-specific; broadcast is FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
MAC addresses are Layer 2 and only matter within one network segment; IP addresses are Layer 3 and are end to end; the MAC pair is rewritten at every router hop while the IP pair stays the same
Hub vs switch: a hub repeats every frame out all ports (one collision domain); a switch forwards by destination MAC and gives each port its own collision domain

chapters.title: How a Switch Builds and Uses Its MAC Table
points: Learning: the switch reads the SOURCE MAC of each incoming frame and records MAC -> ingress port in the MAC (CAM) table
Forwarding: look up the DESTINATION MAC; known unicast goes out only that port; the frame is never sent back out its ingress port
Unknown unicast and broadcast frames are flooded out every port in the VLAN except the ingress port
Entries age out after an idle timeout (default 300 s on Cisco); a host that moves ports is relearned from its next frame
Example: PC-A sends to PC-B while the table is empty, so the frame floods; B replies, the switch learns B's port, and later A to B traffic is forwarded on one port only
Common mistake: a switch never learns from the destination MAC, and a broadcast address can never be a source, so it is never in the table

chapters.title: ARP: Resolving IP to MAC
points: ARP maps a known next-hop IPv4 address to a MAC address on the same subnet; it runs between Layer 2 and Layer 3 and is carried directly in Ethernet (EtherType 0x0806)
Request: broadcast to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF asking 'Who has 10.0.0.5? Tell 10.0.0.2'; Reply: unicast from the owner saying '10.0.0.5 is at AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF'
Flow for sending: same subnet -> ARP for the destination IP; different subnet -> ARP for the default gateway's IP, then send the frame to the gateway's MAC
The ARP cache stores IP -> MAC entries for a limited time (minutes, OS dependent) so each packet doesn't trigger a new request; the receiver also caches the sender's mapping from the request
Gratuitous ARP: a host announces its own IP -> MAC to refresh caches and detect duplicate IPs; ARP has no authentication, so ARP spoofing can poison caches (mitigated by Dynamic ARP Inspection)

chapters.title: ARP and Switch Commands in Practice
points: Show the ARP cache: `arp -a` (Windows/macOS/Linux) or `ip neigh show` (Linux); states include REACHABLE, STALE and FAILED
Clear a stale or wrong entry: `arp -d <ip>` (Windows/Linux) or `sudo ip neigh flush all`
Add a static entry: `arp -s 10.0.0.5 aa-bb-cc-dd-ee-ff` (permanent, survives aging but must be maintained by hand)
Show a host's own MAC and addresses: `ip link show` (Linux) or `ipconfig /all` (Windows)
Cisco switch: `show mac address-table` lists VLAN, MAC, type and port; `clear mac address-table dynamic` flushes learned entries

chapters.title: VLANs, Trunking and Broadcast Domains
points: A broadcast domain is every device that receives a Layer 2 broadcast; switches do not split it, routers do, and each VLAN is its own broadcast domain
A VLAN logically splits one physical switch into separate Layer 2 networks; hosts in different VLANs cannot talk without a Layer 3 device (router or SVI)
Access port: belongs to exactly one VLAN and carries untagged frames; trunk port: carries many VLANs between switches using an 802.1Q tag (4 bytes, 12-bit VLAN ID, range 1-4094)
The native VLAN's frames cross a trunk untagged (default VLAN 1); a native VLAN mismatch between trunk ends causes leaks and warnings, so match it and move it off VLAN 1
Cisco config: `interface g0/1` / `switchport mode access` / `switchport access vlan 10`; trunk: `switchport mode trunk` / `switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20`
Rule of thumb: one VLAN per subnet, with inter-VLAN routing through a router-on-a-stick or a Layer 3 switch

chapters.title: Layer 2 Cheat Sheet
points: Frame: Dst MAC 6B | Src MAC 6B | EtherType 2B | Payload 46-1500B | FCS 4B; broadcast MAC = FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
Switch rules: learn from source MAC, forward by destination MAC, flood unknown unicast and broadcast, aging 300 s
ARP: request is broadcast, reply is unicast; off-subnet traffic ARPs for the gateway; cache with `arp -a` or `ip neigh`
VLAN: access = one VLAN untagged, trunk = many VLANs with 802.1Q tag; each VLAN is one broadcast domain and needs a router to reach another
Mistakes to avoid: native VLAN mismatch, assuming switches stop broadcasts, expecting different VLANs to ping without routing, trusting ARP replies blindly
